questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes advanced midwifery assessment?

choices.text: A systematic evaluation of maternal and fetal health using clinical history, physical examination and appropriate investigations
The routine recording of maternal weight without further examination
The assessment of the fetus without considering maternal health
The administration of medication before obtaining a clinical history

questions.rationale: Advanced midwifery assessment integrates history-taking, physical examination, maternal observations, fetal assessment and relevant investigations. It supports early identification of complications and appropriate clinical decisions.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks' gestation attends a district hospital with severe headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Normal discomforts of late pregnancy
Hyperemesis gravidarum
Severe pre-eclampsia with possible impending eclampsia
Physiological anaemia of pregnancy

questions.rationale: Severe headache, visual disturbances and epigastric pain are warning features of severe pre-eclampsia. The woman requires urgent assessment, maternal and fetal monitoring and management according to the emergency obstetric protocol.

questions.question_text: Which clinical measurement is most important for assessing the severity of hypertension in a pregnant woman?

choices.text: Maternal height
Blood pressure
Abdominal circumference
Mid-upper arm circumference

questions.rationale: Blood pressure measurement is essential in identifying and monitoring hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. Accurate technique and repeat measurements are important when assessing suspected hypertension.

questions.question_text: A woman at 32 weeks' gestation reports that fetal movements have reduced considerably since the previous day. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Reassure her that reduced fetal movement is expected in the third trimester
Advise her to wait until the next antenatal appointment
Recommend increased fluid intake and no further assessment
Arrange prompt assessment of fetal wellbeing, including fetal heart rate evaluation

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement may indicate fetal compromise and requires prompt assessment. The midwife should not dismiss the complaint or delay evaluation until the next routine visit.

questions.question_text: Which investigation is commonly used to assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume when a pregnancy complication is suspected?

choices.text: Obstetric ultrasound examination
Maternal stool microscopy
Electrocardiography of the mother alone
Urine culture only

questions.rationale: Obstetric ultrasound can assess fetal biometry, estimated fetal weight, amniotic fluid volume and other aspects of fetal wellbeing. Findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical assessment.

questions.question_text: A woman at 36 weeks' gestation presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial clinical suspicion?

choices.text: Uterine rupture
Placenta praevia
Normal bloody show
Hyperemesis gravidarum

questions.rationale: Painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy is a classical presentation of placenta praevia. The midwife should assess maternal stability and fetal wellbeing and avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain and a rigid, tender uterus. Her blood pressure is falling. Which condition should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Placenta praevia without complications
Physiological uterine contractions
Abruptio placentae with possible maternal haemorrhage
Braxton Hicks contractions

questions.rationale: Painful bleeding, uterine tenderness and rigidity are characteristic features of placental abruption. Falling blood pressure suggests haemodynamic compromise, requiring urgent resuscitation and obstetric intervention.

questions.question_text: Which maternal observation is particularly useful for detecting early deterioration in a woman with suspected obstetric sepsis?

choices.text: Hair condition
Nail length
Maternal shoe size
Respiratory rate

questions.rationale: Respiratory rate is an important indicator of physiological deterioration and may become abnormal early in severe infection. It should be assessed alongside temperature, pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and mental status.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a maternal temperature of 39°C, pulse rate of 124 beats per minute and uterine tenderness. What is the priority nursing action?

choices.text: Suspect infection, initiate urgent assessment and escalate for prompt obstetric management
Encourage her to sleep and reassess after delivery
Document the findings as normal labour changes
Administer an oral analgesic and discharge her

questions.rationale: Fever, tachycardia and uterine tenderness raise concern for intra-amniotic infection or another serious infection. Prompt clinical assessment, appropriate investigations and timely treatment are necessary to reduce maternal and fetal complications.

questions.question_text: Which condition is characterised by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy accompanied by proteinuria or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction?

choices.text: Gestational diabetes mellitus
Pre-eclampsia
Placenta praevia
Hyperemesis gravidarum

questions.rationale: Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive disorder that develops after 20 weeks of gestation and may involve proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction. It can progress to life-threatening complications affecting the mother and fetus.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. What is the immediate priority?

choices.text: Insert a tongue depressor between her teeth
Restrain her limbs firmly to stop the movements
Protect her from injury, maintain airway and breathing, and summon emergency assistance
Give oral fluids immediately

questions.rationale: During an eclamptic seizure, the midwife should protect the woman from injury, position her to support airway protection when possible and summon emergency assistance. Nothing should be placed in her mouth, and urgent anticonvulsant and obstetric management must follow.

questions.question_text: Which medication is the first-line anticonvulsant for the prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures in standard obstetric practice?

choices.text: Magnesium sulphate
Oxytocin
Ferrous sulphate
Misoprostol

questions.rationale: Magnesium sulphate is the recommended first-line anticonvulsant for eclampsia and prevention of seizures in severe pre-eclampsia. It requires careful administration and monitoring for toxicity, including respiratory depression and reduced reflexes.

questions.question_text: A woman receiving magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia has absent patellar reflexes, a respiratory rate of 9 breaths per minute and reduced urine output. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Increase the magnesium sulphate infusion rate
Encourage the woman to walk around
Continue treatment because these are expected therapeutic effects
Stop magnesium sulphate administration, call for urgent assistance and prepare for toxicity management

questions.rationale: Absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and oliguria suggest magnesium sulphate toxicity. Administration should be stopped and urgent clinical management initiated, including preparation of the prescribed antidote, calcium gluconate, according to protocol.

questions.question_text: Which clinical finding is most suggestive of hypovolaemic shock following obstetric haemorrhage?

choices.text: Warm extremities and a slow pulse
Tachycardia, hypotension and altered mental status
Normal blood pressure with no symptoms
Increased appetite and excessive salivation

questions.rationale: Hypovolaemic shock results from significant loss of circulating blood volume. Tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness and poor peripheral perfusion are important signs of deterioration.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman develops sudden breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia and oxygen desaturation. Which serious complication should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Normal postpartum uterine involution
Physiological breast engorgement
Pulmonary embolism
Uncomplicated afterpains

questions.rationale: Sudden dyspnoea, chest pain, tachycardia and hypoxaemia in the postpartum period are concerning for pulmonary embolism. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate escalation, supportive care and urgent definitive assessment.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman has heavy vaginal bleeding, a weak rapid pulse and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Initiate the postpartum haemorrhage emergency response, call for help and begin resuscitation
Wait for laboratory results before intervening
Encourage the woman to stand and walk
Arrange routine discharge documentation

questions.rationale: Heavy bleeding with hypotension and tachycardia indicates severe haemorrhage with possible shock. Immediate coordinated emergency management, including haemorrhage control, resuscitation and escalation, is essential.

questions.question_text: Which parameter is particularly important when monitoring a critically ill obstetric patient for renal perfusion and fluid balance?

choices.text: Hair growth
Skin pigmentation
Maternal height
Hourly urine output

questions.rationale: Urine output provides useful information about renal perfusion and fluid status in critically ill patients. Persistent oliguria may indicate inadequate circulation, renal impairment or other serious complications.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with suspected sepsis is confused, hypotensive and tachypnoeic. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Delay treatment until the source of infection is confirmed by culture
Initiate urgent sepsis management, escalate care and arrange prompt administration of prescribed treatment
Give oral fluids only and review the following day
Discharge the woman because confusion is unrelated to infection

questions.rationale: Confusion, hypotension and tachypnoea suggest severe infection with possible organ dysfunction. Sepsis management must begin urgently, with appropriate cultures and investigations obtained without delaying time-critical treatment.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes an episiotomy?

choices.text: A surgical incision made in the perineum to enlarge the vaginal outlet during childbirth
A spontaneous separation of the uterine wall
A surgical incision made in the abdominal wall during caesarean section
A tear involving the cervix during labour

questions.rationale: An episiotomy is a deliberate surgical incision of the perineum and vaginal wall performed when clinically indicated. It is not recommended as a routine procedure for every vaginal birth.

questions.question_text: A woman develops severe perineal pain and increasing swelling several hours after an episiotomy. Her pulse rate is elevated. What complication should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Normal wound healing
Uncomplicated lochia
Perineal haematoma
Physiological uterine involution

questions.rationale: Severe perineal pain, swelling and tachycardia after birth may indicate a concealed perineal haematoma. Urgent assessment is required because significant blood loss can occur without obvious external bleeding.

questions.question_text: Which classification describes a third-degree perineal tear?

choices.text: Injury involving the vaginal mucosa and perineal skin only
Injury involving the perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter
Injury extending through the anal sphincter complex into the anorectal mucosa
Injury involving the anal sphincter complex without extension into the anorectal mucosa

questions.rationale: A third-degree tear involves the anal sphincter complex and is subdivided according to the extent of external and internal sphincter involvement. Extension into the anorectal mucosa defines a fourth-degree tear.

questions.question_text: A woman has a fourth-degree perineal tear following vaginal birth. Which management is most appropriate?

choices.text: Allow the wound to heal without repair
Arrange repair by an appropriately trained clinician in a suitable setting, followed by structured postoperative care
Apply an external dressing only and discharge immediately
Suture only the perineal skin without assessing the anal sphincter or anorectal mucosa

questions.rationale: A fourth-degree tear involves the anal sphincter complex and anorectal mucosa and requires specialist repair by a suitably trained clinician. Postoperative care includes appropriate analgesia, bowel management, wound review and follow-up for continence symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which finding is most suggestive of infection in a caesarean section wound?

choices.text: Mild tenderness that is steadily improving
A clean, dry incision with approximated edges
Increasing redness, warmth, purulent discharge and worsening pain
A small amount of bruising that is resolving

questions.rationale: Increasing redness, warmth, pain and purulent discharge are characteristic signs of surgical wound infection. The wound requires clinical assessment and appropriate treatment to prevent progression.

questions.question_text: A woman on the second day after caesarean section reports increasing wound pain. The incision is red and has purulent discharge, and she has a fever. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Assess the wound and vital signs, escalate for clinical review and follow the prescribed infection management plan
Cover the wound and ignore the fever
Tell the woman to remove the sutures herself
Apply an unprescribed herbal preparation to the incision

questions.rationale: Fever, purulent discharge and increasing wound pain suggest a postoperative surgical site infection. Prompt assessment and appropriate treatment are necessary to prevent wound breakdown and systemic infection.

questions.question_text: Which practice is most appropriate when performing a dressing change on a caesarean section wound?

choices.text: Reuse a contaminated dressing if it appears dry
Touch the wound directly with unwashed hands
Clean the wound using any household chemical available
Perform hand hygiene, use appropriate aseptic technique and assess the wound before applying a suitable dressing

questions.rationale: Aseptic technique reduces the risk of introducing microorganisms into the surgical wound. Wound assessment should include the incision edges, surrounding skin, discharge, odour and signs of infection.

questions.question_text: A woman who sustained an episiotomy reports difficulty passing urine and increasing perineal discomfort. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Assume the symptoms are normal and provide no further care
Assess bladder function, perineal condition and pain, and arrange further clinical review as indicated
Restrict all oral fluids
Advise her to avoid passing urine for the rest of the day

questions.rationale: Perineal trauma, pain and oedema may contribute to postpartum urinary retention. Early assessment and appropriate management help prevent bladder overdistension and further complications.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman has a rapidly expanding perineal swelling, severe pain, pallor and hypotension. What is the priority action?

choices.text: Apply a routine perineal dressing and review after several hours
Encourage oral fluids and ambulation
Suspect a significant haematoma, activate emergency assistance and initiate resuscitation
Reassure her that swelling is always expected after vaginal birth

questions.rationale: Rapidly expanding swelling with pallor and hypotension suggests significant concealed haemorrhage from a genital tract haematoma. Immediate escalation, resuscitation and urgent obstetric intervention are required.

questions.question_text: Which definition best describes primary postpartum haemorrhage?

choices.text: Bleeding occurring only during the first stage of labour
Any vaginal bleeding occurring after six weeks postpartum
Bleeding occurring before the delivery of the placenta
Excessive bleeding within the first 24 hours after birth

questions.rationale: Primary postpartum haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours after birth. It is a major obstetric emergency, and management should be initiated promptly when excessive bleeding or signs of haemodynamic compromise are identified.

questions.question_text: A woman develops heavy bleeding immediately after vaginal birth. The uterus is enlarged, soft and poorly contracted. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Uterine atony
Cervical ectropion
Normal lochia
Urinary tract infection

questions.rationale: Uterine atony occurs when the uterus fails to contract effectively after birth, allowing continued bleeding from the placental bed. It is a leading cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.question_text: A woman experiences postpartum haemorrhage and the uterus is boggy. Which action should the midwife take immediately while activating the haemorrhage response?

choices.text: Ask the woman to walk to the toilet
Perform uterine massage to encourage contraction and assess the response
Delay intervention until the haemoglobin result is available
Apply pressure to the woman's chest

questions.rationale: Uterine massage is an immediate intervention for a boggy uterus associated with postpartum haemorrhage. It should occur alongside urgent help, assessment of the cause, resuscitation and administration of prescribed uterotonic treatment.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour develops shoulder dystocia after delivery of the fetal head. Which manoeuvre is commonly used as an initial intervention?

choices.text: Fundal pressure
Kristeller manoeuvre
McRoberts manoeuvre
External cephalic version

questions.rationale: The McRoberts manoeuvre involves hyperflexion of the mother's hips to flatten the sacrum and facilitate release of the impacted shoulder. Fundal pressure should not be used because it can worsen shoulder impaction and cause injury.

questions.question_text: During shoulder dystocia, the midwife is assisting with the emergency response. Which action should be avoided?

choices.text: Calling for additional skilled assistance
Preparing for neonatal resuscitation
Recording the time of delivery of the fetal head
Applying fundal pressure to force delivery of the shoulders

questions.rationale: Fundal pressure can worsen shoulder impaction and increase the risk of maternal and neonatal injury. The team should use recognised shoulder dystocia manoeuvres in an organised sequence and document the events.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a prolapsed umbilical cord following spontaneous rupture of membranes. The fetal heart rate is severely reduced. What is the immediate priority?

choices.text: Arrange urgent assistance and relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part while preparing for emergency birth
Push the cord back into the uterus
Ask the woman to walk around to encourage descent
Wait for the next routine fetal heart assessment

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse can cause acute fetal hypoxia through compression of the umbilical cord. The presenting part should be elevated to relieve compression, the cord should not be replaced into the uterus, and emergency delivery should be arranged.

questions.question_text: A woman with cord prolapse is awaiting emergency caesarean section. Which maternal position can help reduce pressure on the prolapsed cord?

choices.text: Standing upright
Knee-chest position or a left lateral position with the pelvis elevated
Flat supine position without pelvic elevation
Sitting upright with legs hanging down

questions.rationale: The knee-chest position or an appropriate lateral position with pelvic elevation can reduce compression of the prolapsed cord. These measures are temporary while urgent definitive delivery is arranged.

questions.question_text: A woman with eclampsia is admitted to a district hospital after a seizure. She remains unconscious and has noisy breathing. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Obtain the woman's antenatal card before providing care
Administer oral antihypertensive medication
Maintain airway patency, support breathing and summon emergency assistance
Begin routine breastfeeding counselling

questions.rationale: An unconscious woman with noisy breathing is at risk of airway obstruction and aspiration. Airway and breathing management take priority while the team continues seizure control, maternal stabilisation and obstetric management.

questions.question_text: A woman develops postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean section. The uterus is firm, but bleeding continues. Which cause should the midwife consider?

choices.text: Uterine atony as the only possible cause
Normal postpartum uterine involution
Breast engorgement
Genital tract trauma, retained tissue or a coagulation disorder

questions.rationale: Persistent bleeding despite a firm uterus suggests that causes other than uterine atony must be considered. The midwife should support prompt assessment for trauma, retained placental tissue and coagulopathy while continuing haemorrhage management.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, cessation of contractions and loss of the previously palpable fetal presenting part. Her pulse is rapid and blood pressure is falling. What complication should be suspected?

choices.text: Uterine rupture
Normal transition phase of labour
Uncomplicated cervical dilatation
Physiological fetal descent

questions.rationale: Sudden abdominal pain, maternal shock, altered uterine activity and loss of fetal station are concerning features of uterine rupture. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent operative management.

questions.question_text: A woman develops severe bleeding after birth and the placenta is not delivered. The uterus is not palpable in its normal abdominal position, and a mass is visible at the vaginal opening. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Uncomplicated retained placenta
Uterine inversion
Normal uterine involution
Cervical insufficiency

questions.rationale: Uterine inversion may present with severe haemorrhage, shock and absence of the uterine fundus in its normal abdominal position. It requires immediate emergency assistance and prompt specialist management.

questions.question_text: What is the primary goal of palliative care for a woman with a life-limiting obstetric or medical condition?

choices.text: To withdraw all forms of communication with the family
To provide comfort, relieve suffering and support quality of life
To guarantee that the underlying disease will be cured
To avoid discussing the patient's symptoms

questions.rationale: Palliative care aims to prevent and relieve suffering through early identification and management of physical, psychosocial and spiritual needs. It supports quality of life for the patient and family and is not limited to the final hours of life.

questions.question_text: A woman with advanced cancer complicating pregnancy has chosen comfort-focused care after informed discussions with her clinical team. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Ignore her symptoms because curative treatment is no longer the main goal
Pressure her to accept every available intervention
Provide symptom relief, emotional support and care consistent with her informed preferences
Exclude her from all decisions about her care

questions.rationale: Comfort-focused care requires active management of pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety and other distressing symptoms. The care plan should respect the woman's informed preferences and involve appropriate multidisciplinary support.

questions.question_text: A mother experiences stillbirth and begins crying uncontrollably. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?

choices.text: Allow her to express her grief, listen empathetically and offer appropriate bereavement support
Tell her that she should stop crying because she can have another baby
Avoid speaking to her until she becomes calm
Tell her that grieving is a sign of weakness

questions.rationale: Bereavement care requires empathy, active listening and acknowledgement of the family's loss. The midwife should provide emotional support and explain available bereavement services without minimising the parents' grief.

questions.question_text: Which action is most important when providing end-of-life care to a woman who is conscious and able to make her own healthcare decisions?

choices.text: Allow relatives to make every decision without consulting her
Withhold information about her condition
Make decisions based only on the healthcare team's preferences
Respect her autonomy, explain care options and support informed decision-making

questions.rationale: A competent patient retains the right to receive information and participate in decisions about her care. Respecting autonomy includes discussing preferences, goals of care and appropriate treatment options.

questions.question_text: A woman receiving palliative care reports severe uncontrolled pain. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Tell her that pain is unavoidable in advanced illness
Assess the pain, promptly report uncontrolled symptoms and implement the prescribed pain management plan
Withhold analgesia to avoid possible dependence
Ask the family to manage the pain without clinical guidance

questions.rationale: Pain relief is a central component of palliative care and should not be withheld solely because a patient has advanced illness. The midwife should assess pain systematically and support timely, appropriate analgesic management.

questions.question_text: Following a maternal death, relatives become distressed and accuse the healthcare team of failing to provide adequate care. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Argue with the relatives to defend the hospital
Leave the relatives without any explanation or support
Respond with compassion, maintain confidentiality and facilitate appropriate communication with the responsible clinical team
Disclose confidential information about other patients to justify the care provided

questions.rationale: Families affected by maternal death require compassionate communication and appropriate bereavement support. Questions about clinical care should be addressed through the responsible team using respectful, factual and confidential communication.

questions.question_text: What is clinical decision-making in midwifery?

choices.text: Choosing interventions based only on personal experience
Making decisions without assessing the patient
Following routine instructions regardless of the woman's condition
Using clinical assessment, evidence, professional judgement and the woman's preferences to guide care

questions.rationale: Clinical decision-making integrates assessment findings, current evidence, professional competence and patient preferences. It supports safe, individualised and timely midwifery care.

questions.question_text: A midwife in a CHPS compound assesses a pregnant woman with severe vaginal bleeding and signs of shock. The facility does not have the capacity for emergency surgery. What is the most appropriate decision?

choices.text: Arrange urgent referral to an appropriate hospital while initiating stabilisation and communicating with the receiving facility
Keep the woman at the CHPS compound until all investigations are completed
Discharge her with advice to return if bleeding continues
Wait for a routine review by the district health directorate

questions.rationale: Severe bleeding with shock requires emergency management beyond the capacity of a basic facility. Stabilisation, prompt referral, pre-referral communication and safe transfer are essential to reduce maternal mortality.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a persistent abnormal fetal heart rate pattern despite initial corrective measures. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Continue routine monitoring without informing the obstetric team
Recognise possible fetal compromise, escalate immediately and prepare for expedited birth as clinically indicated
Ask the woman to go home and return the following day
Stop monitoring because the fetal heart rate has already been assessed

questions.rationale: A persistent abnormal fetal heart rate pattern may indicate fetal compromise requiring urgent assessment. The midwife should escalate promptly and support timely decisions about the safest mode and timing of birth.

questions.question_text: A woman at a district hospital has prolonged labour, maternal exhaustion and no progress in cervical dilatation despite adequate contractions. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Normal progress in the active phase
Uncomplicated latent labour
Obstructed labour or another cause of labour dystocia requiring urgent assessment
Normal postpartum involution

questions.rationale: Failure of labour to progress despite adequate contractions raises concern for labour dystocia, including possible obstruction. The midwife should assess maternal and fetal wellbeing and escalate for an appropriate obstetric management decision.

questions.question_text: A woman with suspected ectopic pregnancy presents with severe lower abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness and hypotension. What is the priority decision?

choices.text: Arrange routine outpatient review in one week
Provide reassurance and advise rest at home
Give oral iron and schedule antenatal registration
Suspect ruptured ectopic pregnancy and arrange immediate emergency management and referral

questions.rationale: Severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain and hypotension may indicate intraperitoneal bleeding from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent surgical assessment.

questions.question_text: A midwife is uncertain whether a woman's postpartum bleeding is within normal limits. Which action best demonstrates safe clinical decision-making?

choices.text: Assess the amount and pattern of bleeding, uterine tone and vital signs, then seek senior review if concerned
Assume that all bleeding after birth is normal
Wait until the woman becomes unconscious before taking action
Discharge the woman without documenting the findings

questions.rationale: Postpartum bleeding must be assessed in relation to its amount, clinical pattern and the woman's physiological condition. Early recognition of abnormal bleeding and timely escalation can prevent progression to severe haemorrhage.

questions.question_text: A midwife is caring for a woman with suspected placenta praevia and vaginal bleeding. Which examination should be avoided until placenta praevia has been excluded?

choices.text: Measurement of maternal blood pressure
Digital vaginal examination
Assessment of maternal pulse
Fetal heart rate assessment

questions.rationale: Digital vaginal examination may disrupt a placenta lying over or near the cervical opening and precipitate severe haemorrhage. Maternal stabilisation and fetal assessment should proceed while the placental location is established using appropriate methods.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe anaemia in late pregnancy presents with breathlessness at rest, chest discomfort and marked tachycardia. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Advise her to increase dietary iron and return in one month
Assume the symptoms are normal effects of pregnancy
Assess airway, breathing and circulation, escalate urgently and arrange appropriate medical management
Discharge her because anaemia is common in pregnancy

questions.rationale: Breathlessness at rest, chest discomfort and marked tachycardia may indicate severe physiological compromise in a woman with anaemia. Immediate assessment and escalation are required rather than relying on routine dietary advice.

questions.question_text: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage continues to bleed despite initial treatment. Her blood pressure is falling and she is becoming confused. Which decision is most appropriate?

choices.text: Continue routine observation because confusion is expected after delivery
Wait for the next scheduled ward round
Stop monitoring once intravenous fluids have been commenced
Escalate immediately for advanced haemorrhage management, blood products and definitive intervention as indicated

questions.rationale: Persistent bleeding with hypotension and confusion indicates worsening haemorrhagic shock. The woman requires urgent escalation, ongoing resuscitation and definitive control of the bleeding source.

questions.question_text: Which action is most important when transferring a critically ill obstetric patient from a district hospital to a regional hospital?

choices.text: Stabilise the patient as far as possible, arrange appropriate transport and provide a structured clinical handover
Send the patient without clinical information to save time
Delay transfer until the patient is completely stable, regardless of available resources
Allow the patient to travel alone without appropriate monitoring or support

questions.rationale: Safe referral requires prompt communication, appropriate pre-transfer stabilisation, suitable transport and a clear handover of clinical findings and interventions. Transfer should not be unnecessarily delayed while waiting for complete stabilisation when definitive care is unavailable.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a temperature of 38.8°C, maternal tachycardia and fetal tachycardia. Membranes ruptured several hours earlier. Which interpretation should guide the midwife's next action?

choices.text: The findings are normal and require no further assessment
The findings raise concern for intra-amniotic infection and require urgent clinical assessment and escalation
Fetal tachycardia always indicates a normal response to labour
The woman should be discharged because the membranes have ruptured

questions.rationale: Maternal fever and tachycardia with fetal tachycardia after rupture of membranes raise concern for intra-amniotic infection. Prompt assessment and appropriate treatment are necessary to reduce the risk of maternal and neonatal complications.
